2. A simple application for restoration has lingered
on for the past 19 years.
3. Brief facts are that the petitioners claimed to
have purchased lands from the original respondent Nos. 4,
5 and M/s.Maqsood and Maqdoom Benefit Trust in 1991. For
the purpose of disposal of this matter, it is enough if
we refer to the suits filed in 2002. On 28th October,
2002, OS No. 7295 of 2002, OS No. 7296 of 2002, and OS
No. 7297 of 2002 were filed by respondent Nos. 1 to 3 and
others against the petitioners and respondent Nos.4 and
5, claiming that the properties belonging to a Trust have
been  illegally  alienated.  The  sale  deed  dated  26th
November,  1991,  under  which  the  properties  were
purchased, was directly called in question.
4. On 29th October, 2007, the Trial Court dismissed OS
No. 7295 of 2002 for default. 
5. On 2nd November 2007, Misc.Petition No. 850 of 2007
was filed by the plaintiffs, seeking restoration of OS
No. 7295 of 2002.
6. It is this petition which ultimately came to be
allowed by the Trial Court on 31st October, 2013, and the
said restoration has been confirmed by the High Court, by
the impugned order, in revision.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.1074/2015
NEERAJ KUMAR                                  Appellant(s)
                           VERSUS
SURAJ PRAKASH & ORS.                          Respondent(s)
O R D E R
1.This is a complainant’s appeal against the judgment
and order of the High Court1 dismissing the revision
of the complainant against the judgment and order of
the  Trial  Court2 whereby  the  respondents  were
acquitted of the charge of dowry death, punishable
under Section 304B of the Indian Penal Code, 1860
(IPC), and of cruelty, punishable under Section 498A
IPC.
2.The Trial Court while acquitting the respondents had
found that the evidence in respect of demand of dowry
and  harassment  in  connection  therewith  was  not
reliable and except ante-mortem burn injuries, no
other injury referable to use of force was found. It
1 1 High Court of Delhi at New Delhi
2 2 Additional Sessions Judge
1

--- Page 34 ---
also took into consideration the financial position of
the complainant-party as also the statement of the
employer of the brother of the deceased, who was the
only earning member in the complainant’s family, that
the brother of the deceased was drawing a meagre
salary of Rs.2,300/- per month, to disbelieve the
allegations of demand of a handsome amount towards
dowry. Based upon consideration of the entire evidence
on record as also the fact that initially there were
differences between the husband and wife on account of
some suspicion in the mind of the husband that the
wife had been pregnant since before marriage and
husband had also filed for divorce, though later
withdrawn, the Trial Court concluded that harassment
for demand of dowry was not proved and there was no
cogent evidence to convict the accused for dowry death
by raising a presumption under Section 113B of the
Evidence Act. 
3.Aggrieved  by  the  acquittal  of  the  accused  i.e.
respondents, the complainant preferred a revision.
Notably, there was no State appeal against the order
of  acquittal.   The  High  Court  scrutinized  the
evidence, particularly of PW-1 (i.e. mother of the
2

--- Page 35 ---
deceased), PW-2 (i.e. elder brother of the deceased)
and PW-8 (i.e. younger brother of the deceased) to
observe that none of them stated that there had been a
demand of dowry at the time of marriage; besides there
had been some improvement in the testimony of PW-1
from what she had stated during investigation. The
Court also took notice of the fact that a panchayat
was held earlier to resolve the differences between
husband and wife, and documents prepared in connection
therewith do not reflect any demand of dowry.
4.Having regard to the evidence brought on record as
also the financial position of the complainant family,
the High Court was of the view that there was no
perversity in the assessment of evidence by the Trial
Court while rendering the decision of acquittal, and
therefore, no case for interference in revisional
jurisdiction was made out.
5.Impugning the aforesaid judgments, the learned counsel
for the complainant has submitted that the courts
below have committed an error in taking a view that
PW-1 i.e. mother of the deceased had improved upon her
previous  statement.  It  has  been  submitted  that,
firstly, the previous statement of PW-1 has not been
3

--- Page 36 ---
extracted while recording her testimony and, secondly,
there  is  no  improvement  pointed  out  except  that
earlier she had not made a statement to that effect.
It has been submitted that if the statement of PW-1 is
read in its entirety it would indicate that she is
consistent about demand of dowry and that demand was
repeated soon before the death of the deceased. This
is clear from her statement where she stated that just
two days before death of her daughter, she had gone to
the house of her daughter to give certain gifts on the
eve of Ganga Snan. PW-1 stated that then her daughter
had asked her whether she had brought money or not and
when  PW-1  replied  in  the  negative,  her  daughter
started weeping and requested PW-1 to take her back
home. She also stated that husband of the deceased had
slapped  the  deceased  two  or  three  times  in  her
presence. PW-1 also stated that she had called her son
(PW-8), namely, Sanjay, who then came to take her back
home. However, during cross-examination PW-1 stated
that she did not remember whether she had told the
police  that  on  08.06.1995,  she  had  come  to  her
daughter’s house. Further, she stated that she had not
stated to the police that husband of the deceased had
slapped the deceased two or three times. She had also
4

--- Page 37 ---
not stated that she had called over her younger son
Sanjay to fetch her. These circumstances, according to
the appellant’s counsel, were not such which could
completely discredit the testimony of PW-1. 
6.Appellant’s counsel further submitted that the Court
had failed to consider the recital in the inquest
report to the effect that an incised wound was present
on the forehead of the deceased. This, according to
him, was a relevant piece of evidence which was
completely overlooked by the Trial Court as well as
the High Court and, therefore, their decision is
liable to be set aside.   
7.Additionally, it has been submitted that it is not
necessary to prove that the relative upon whom demand
is made had the capacity to meet the demand. What is
required  to  be  proved  is  that  there  had  been
harassment in connection with demand of dowry. It has
been  submitted  that  the  evidence  led  by  the
prosecution had clearly established that there was
harassment  in  connection  with  demand  of  dowry
therefore,  the  benefit  of  the  presumption  was
available to the prosecution, which the Trial Court as
well as the High Court failed to provide.
5

--- Page 38 ---
8.It has also been submitted that besides the aforesaid
three  witnesses,  PW-11,  who  was  mediator  in  the
marriage, had also supported the prosecution case
though  not  much  weightage  was  attached  to  his
testimony. 
9.Per contra, on behalf of the accused-respondents, it
has been submitted that both Trial Court as well as
the  High  Court  considered  the  evidence  of  the
prosecution in detail and found that the allegations
of  demand  of  dowry  and  harassment  in  connection
therewith were not satisfactorily established by the
prosecution. This being a finding of fact, based on
appreciation  of  evidence,  is  not  amenable  to
interference more so when such finding is rendered in
a judgment of acquittal. It is submitted that only a
perverse finding can be interfered with and not a
finding  which  takes  a  possible  view  based  on
appreciation of evidence. It has also been submitted
that  so  far  as  the  allegation  of  presence  of
antemortem injury other than burn injuries on the body
of the deceased is concerned, no such injury has been
found during postmortem and a review opinion was also
sought, which confirmed that there was no injury other
6

--- Page 39 ---
than burn injuries on the body of the deceased.
Besides, the person who sought to prove the inquest
report had not disclosed about noticing any such
injury. Moreover, in the event of there being a
conflict between the autopsy report and the inquest
report, it is the autopsy report which must prevail
and, therefore, the argument that the presence of
injury on the body of the deceased has been ignored is
liable to be rejected. It has also been urged from the
respondents’ side that the evidence brought on record
had clearly established that there were differences
between husband and wife on account of the wife being
found pregnant immediately after marriage. The husband
suspected that she was carrying the pregnancy from
before and in connection therewith a petition was
filed for declaring the marriage void though it was
later withdrawn. Besides, none of the witnesses has
stated that there was any demand of dowry at the time
of marriage. In such circumstances, having regard to
the incapacity of the complainant-party to pay the
kind of dowry allegedly demanded, if the allegations
have been disbelieved, the findings rendered by the
Trial Court, affirmed by the High Court, do not call
for any interference. Hence, it is prayed that the
7

--- Page 40 ---
appeal be dismissed.
10. We have considered the rival submissions and have
perused  the  record  carefully.  Before  we  proceed
further, we may observe that before the revisional
court, during arguments, the learned counsel for the
complainant had not pressed the charge of murder. Only
the charge of dowry death and cruelty/ harassment in
connection with demand of dowry was pressed. No doubt,
death of the deceased was within seven years of her
marriage. However, to raise a presumption either under
Section 113A or Section 113B of the Indian Evidence
Act, 1872, the necessary ingredients would have to be
proved. The foundational fact regarding demand of
dowry and harassment in connection therewith have not
been found proved by the trial court; hence, the
accused were acquitted. 
11. We  notice  that  the  evidence  on  record
substantiates that initially there were differences
between husband and wife emanating from husband’s
suspicion that the wife had been pregnant since before
marriage. This suspicion may be one of the reasons for
the differences between husband and wife, though those
differences got resolved over a period of time and two
8

--- Page 41 ---
more children were born in the wedlock. In such
circumstances, those differences cannot be considered
sufficient as to raise a presumption under Section
113A of the Evidence Act for the purpose of recording
conviction under Section 306 IPC. 
12. Insofar  as  the  benefit  of  presumption  under
Section 113B is concerned, there had to be cogent
evidence in respect of demand of dowry and harassment
in connection therewith soon before death. Here, the
Trial Court had found that such demand of dowry was
not  established  by  cogent  evidence  and  that  the
statement of the prosecution witnesses in that regard
were not reliable. Moreover, lack of capacity to pay
dowry, though by itself may not be sufficient to
disbelieve the accusation of harassment in connection
with demand of dowry, is relevant while assessing the
correctness of the allegation. This we say so because
why would a person raise a demand when he knows that
the person to whom demand is made has no capacity to
fulfil it. Thus, we do not find any perversity in the
assessment of evidence. Once such is the position, and
there is no cogent evidence either to prove murder or
to make such an inference from the circumstances,
9

--- Page 42 ---
taking into account that the Trial Court has taken a
possible view of the matter, which by no means could
be considered perverse, and no appeal was preferred by
the State whereas the Revisional Court’s jurisdiction
is limited, no interference is called for with the
impugned order dismissing revision against acquittal.
13. The appeal is, accordingly, dismissed. 
14. Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall  stand
disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION 
Criminal Appeal No(s).  1675/2019
STATE OF UTTARAKHAND                               Appellant(s)
                                VERSUS
SUDHIR KUMAR SAXENA                                Respondent(s)
O R D E R
1. This appeal is against the judgment
and  order  of  the  High  Court1 dated
09.04.2015  whereby  the  appeal2 of  the
respondent-accused was allowed and he was
acquitted of the charge of murder.
2. The prosecution case in brief was that
on 27.09.2007, post noon, the body of the
deceased was found in open sugar field by
PW-2 of which information was given to the
police  by  PW-1  at  about  3.05  pm.  Upon
receipt of information from newspaper report
1High Court of Uttarakhand at Nainital
22 Criminal Appeal No.267/2010
1

--- Page 45 ---
that a dead body was found, on 28.09.2007,
deceased’s wife lodged a report alleging
that the deceased and the accused had a
quarrel 3-4 days back over money lent by
deceased to the accused; in the morning of
26.09.2007, the deceased was taken from home
by the accused and, thereafter, the deceased
did not return; therefore, she suspects that
the accused has a hand in the murder of the
deceased. Autopsy of the cadaver was held at
about 12:30 hours on 28.09.2007. In the
opinion  of  the  doctor  death  was  a
consequence of antemortem injuries, caused
by sharp-edged weapon, and could have had
occurred  on  or  about  the  evening  of
26.09.2007.
3. During  investigation  blood-stained
clothes of the accused and a Patal (a mini
sword)  was  allegedly  recovered  at  the
instance of the accused-respondent. However,
forensic examination of those articles could
not connect the alleged bloodstains with
either  the  blood  group  or  DNA  of  the
2

--- Page 46 ---
deceased.
4. The prosecution sought to bring home
the charge based on three circumstances,
namely, (a) the accused held the motive for
the murder; (b) the deceased was last seen
alive in the evening of 26.09.2007 in the
company of the accused and, thereafter his
dead body was found on 27.09.2007; and (c)
blood-stained weapon of murder and blood-
stained  clothes  were  recovered  at  the
instance of the accused. 
5. Motive was sought to be proved by
examining  the  wife  of  the  deceased  who
deposed that the deceased had lent money to
the accused and when the deceased demanded
back his money, the accused got annoyed and,
thereafter,  had  a  grudge  against  the
deceased. The last seen evidence is in two
buckets. One is of the deceased being taken
from home by the accused early morning of
26.09.2007. Evidence in that regard comes
from the deceased-wife and a neighbor who
confirms that the deceased was taken in the
3

--- Page 47 ---
morning from home by the accused. However,
this evidence is inconclusive in as much as
it is stated that the deceased and the
accused were seen together having snacks at
a nearby shop. The other bucket of last seen
evidence comes from two witnesses who saw
the  deceased  and  the  accused  together
between 4 pm and 5 p.m. on 26.09.2007.
Interestingly, one of the witnesses of this
circumstance states that he came to know
about  the  death  of  the  deceased  early
morning on the next day at about 10 a.m. But
this  statement  does  not  appear  reliable
because the body was first discovered by PW-
2 post noon of 27.09.2007 and report to that
effect  was  made  by  PW-1  at  3:05pm  on
27.09.2005. Besides, the said witness did
not  disclose  about  the  incriminating
circumstance for as long as 3 days. Apart
from above, those witnesses do not disclose
about any fight between the deceased or the
accused though they allegedly noticed the
two  quarreling  with  each  other.  Having
4

--- Page 48 ---
regard to the nature of the evidence that
was brought on record, the High Court found
that last seen circumstance by its very
nature is a weak type of an evidence and the
witnesses  who  saw  the  deceased  and  the
accused together have not noticed any kind
of weapon being carried by the accused, and
therefore, this was a fit case where the
benefit of doubt must go to the accused.
Consequently, the High Court allowed the
appeal and set aside the order passed by the
Trial Court.
6. The learned counsel representing the
State-appellant submitted that the medical
evidence would indicate that the deceased
was done to death on or about the evening of
26.09.2007, and the accused and the deceased
were seen together on or about that time,
therefore, in absence of any explanation or
evidence by the accused as to when he parted
company  of  the  deceased,  an  adverse
inference ought to be drawn against the
accused by virtue of Section 106 of the
5

--- Page 49 ---
Indian  Evidence  Act,  1872.  In  such
circumstances, there was no justification
for the High Court to reverse the decision
of the Trial Court and acquit the accused.
7. Per contra,  the learned counsel for
the respondent submitted that the High Court
has considered the evidence on record and
the view taken by the High Court is a
possible view which by no means could be
considered  perverse  particularly  having
regard to the nature of the evidence which
the prosecution led before the court. In
such  circumstances,  according  to  the
respondent, there is no justification for
this Court to interfere with the acquittal
order passed by the High Court.
8. We have accorded due consideration to
the rival submissions and have perused the
materials available on record.
9. What is important in this case is that
the testimony of the wife of the deceased
regarding the motive for the crime does not
inspire our confidence in as much as if the
6

--- Page 50 ---
wife was suspecting the accused of harboring
an ill motive against the deceased, she
would not have waited for two long days to
lodge even a missing report. There is no
explanation in her testimony as to why she
did not make any report that her husband has
not returned. Besides, no details of any
money transaction have been disclosed in her
testimony. In such circumstances, even the
motive is not proved beyond doubt. 
10. As far as the evidence of last seen is
concerned, there appears no clear evidence
that the accused was last seen with the
deceased near the place where his body was
found. Even assuming that they were seen
together on or about the same place, there
is huge time gap between the last seen
circumstance  and  discovery  of  the  body.
Ordinarily, last seen circumstance on its
own cannot be the basis of conviction unless
the time-gap between last seen circumstance
and discovery of dead body is so minimal
that involvement of any third person in the
7

--- Page 51 ---
crime is obviated. Moreover, the accused was
not noticed carrying any kind of weapon. 
11. Having regard to the nature of the
evidence brought out by the prosecution as
also the fact that the articles recovered
could not be connected to the blood group of
the deceased, in our view, grant of benefit
of doubt to the accused by the High Court
was a possible view, which does not call for
interference.
12. Accordingly, the appeal is dismissed.
13. Pending application(s), if any, shall
stand disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA 
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION 
 
 
Criminal Appeal No.                of 2026 
[ @ Special Leave Petition (Crl.) No.16804 of 2026 ] 
 
 
Md. Akter Khan @ Bapon Khan 
                     ...Appellant

O R D E R 
Leave granted.  
2. The appellant is aggrieved with the impugned judgment, by 
which the High Court though found the charges under the 
Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012 (POCSO Act) 
to be not sustainable for reason of the age of the prosecutrix not 
having been proved, still upheld the conviction under Section 376 
(1) of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (IPC) and maintained the 
sentence as awarded by the Trial Court, of 15 years of rigorous 
imprisonment with a fine of Rs.50,000/- and a default sentence of 
simple imprisonment for one year. 
3. Prosecution alleged that PW1, the victim was offered a lift in 
a car driven by the accused and later she was taken to two places; 
first an Ethnic Village Park at Jatinga, where she felt dizzy from the 

--- Page 54 ---
Page 2 of 8 
 
soft drink and short eats offered earlier by the accused, in which 
state she was sexually assaulted repeatedly. It was also alleged 
that, then the accused had taken her to another place where again 
he raped her, at which point she totally lost her consciousness. She 
was found unconscious on the roadside from which she was taken 
to the hospital by her brother who was summoned there, by a 
friend. The accused was arrested from his house and after 
investigation, the case was put up for trial in which he was 
convicted and sentenced as hereinabove stated. 
4. We heard Sri Shekhar Prit Jha, learned Advocate-on-Record 
appearing for the appellant and Sri Ankit Roy, learned Advocate-
on-Record appearing for the respondent. 
5. Altogether twenty witnesses were examined, and we have 
gone through the testimonies of the relevant ones as produced in 
the appeal. PW1 was the victim, who deposed that though she 
knew the accused; he being a regular visitor to the house of one of 
her friends, they were formally introduced on 15.08.2019. It is her 
deposition that on 15.08.2019 while she was returning home along 
with PW16, her cousin, the accused came in his car and offered lift. 
On persistent request made, they boarded his car, when he 
introduced himself. On that day, he dropped both at the house of 
the victim, as promised. Two days later, on 17.08.2019, while she 

--- Page 55 ---
Page 3 of 8 
 
was proceeding to the hospital to check on a sick neighbour, the 
accused again came in his car and offered to drop her at the 
hospital. However, he refused to stop the car at the hospital and 
proceeded further and stopped the car near the Cultural Institute 
Hall. He bought her potato chips and coca cola and while 
proceeding further, at his request, she ate the chips and drank the 
soft drink, despite her statement that the drink had a smell 
emanating from it. Ignoring her request to drop her at the civil 
hospital, she was taken first to the Ethnic Village Park, where inside 
the car, she was sexually assaulted repeatedly; allegedly three 
times, and then later taken to another place where she was raped 
again. She claims that she regained consciousness at the hospital. 
The prosecution case was entirely founded on her testimony, and 
we will look at the corroboration attempted by the prosecution 
before the Trial Court. 
6. At the outset, we have to notice that the prosecution was at 
pains to bring forth a confession as elicited from the accused 
through PW4 and PW5; witnesses to the crime scene 
reconstruction, PW7; the photographer who accompanied the 
police team and PW8, the Assistant Commissioner, who also 
accompanied the IO in the crime scene reconstruction. Obviously, 
the confession was made when the accused was in police custody 

--- Page 56 ---
Page 4 of 8 
 
and cannot be relied upon under Section 26 of the Indian Evidence 
Act, 1872. PW5, who was witness to the crime scene reconstruction 
also turned hostile.  
7. In the sequence of events, as put forth by the prosecution, 
PW2, an auto driver was proffered as a witness to indicate that the 
victim was found abandoned on the road in an unconscious state. 
PW2 submits that PW9, the brother of the victim came to the scene 
of occurrence, on being summoned. PW9, the brother of the victim, 
in his deposition said that he was summoned over the phone by a 
friend, who saw his sister lying unconscious on the roadside. He is 
said to have rushed in his auto rickshaw, along with three others; 
another younger sister and a couple to Bagetar, where the victim 
was found lying on the roadside. He is said to have taken her to 
Haflong Civil Hospital for treatment wherein she narrated about the 
incident of her having been taken in the car, made unconscious and 
raped. PW9, also an auto driver, does not speak of the name of the 
friend who summoned him nor of the couple and his other younger 
sister, who accompanied him; none of whom were examined 
before Court. The evidence of PW2, another auto driver, a chance 
witness, regarding the abandonment of the victim, hence, is 
insufficient; especially since none from the crowd gathered, 

--- Page 57 ---
Page 5 of 8 
 
informed the police of the abandoned girl, who was also lying 
unconscious.  
8. The evidence of PW3 is irrelevant, since he claimed to be the 
Secretary of All Assam Gorkha Students Union, Haflong, who had 
visited the victim at the hospital, to whom, the victim is said to have 
narrated the very same allegations. It is also relevant that the crime 
scene reconstruction spoken of by PW4 and PW7 specifically 
speaks of such reconstruction having been done at the Ethnic 
Village Park and at Pan Nala; the second site having not been 
spoken of by PW1 herself. PW6 is the owner of a Pan/Cosmetic 
shop, who merely deposes that the accused, who is the driver of a 
cruiser vehicle, purchased coke and chips from his shop but he 
does not remember the day or the time when such purchase was 
made and he deposes that 2-3 days later, he was informed of the 
accused having been arrested for the rape of a girl. The evidence 
of PW7 and PW8, who accompanied the IO, at the time of 
reconstruction of the crime scene, as already found is irrelevant. 
PW10 is the father of the accused and PW15 is the uncle of the 
victim who does not depose anything about the crime as such. 
9. Relevant is the deposition of PW16, who is said to have 
accompanied the victim on 15.10.2018 when both were picked up 
by the accused in his car. While PW1, the victim stated that on the 

--- Page 58 ---
Page 6 of 8 
 
said day, herself and PW16 were dropped in front of her house by 
the accused, PW16 had a different version. PW16 says that without 
taking them towards their home, the accused drove the car around 
Haflong town and took them to Ethnic Village near Jatinga and after 
repeated requests, they were dropped near Dimasa Mandir Surat 
Nagar, Haflong. The version of PW16 differs considerably from that 
of PW1, the victim. The conduct of the accused, on the previous 
occasion, as spoken of by PW16, if true, should have cautioned the 
victim on the next occasion.  
10. Further, it is to be reiterated that the deposition of PW1 
indicates that she was not only sexually assaulted but also beaten 
up inside the car and the accused had forceful sexual intercourse 
with her 2-3 times inside the car at the Ethnic Village Par. Again, 
she deposes that she was taken to another place; the location not 
being indicated, where she was again raped. The medical 
evidence, hence, assumes significance insofar as the specific 
allegations raised. PW17, a Psychiatrist, who examined her mental 
condition did not depose anything with respect to the crime proper 
as such. The Doctor who examined her on 19.08.2019, testified as 
PW20 before the Trial Court. The examination revealed that there 
were no minor or major injuries on any part of the body of the 
victim nor was there any sign of sexual intercourse present. Her 

--- Page 59 ---
Page 7 of 8 
 
age as per the X-Ray findings were approximately 18 to 19 years 
and there was no sign of spermatozoa on the vaginal swab and 
there was no violation mark detected. The allegations of forceful 
sexual assault on more than three occasions and the allegation of 
beating up inside the car are not supported by the medical 
evidence. Despite the fact that the witness was examined two days 
after the incident, the complete absence of any signs of assault and 
forceful intercourse raises a reasonable doubt. 
11.  Pertinent also is the fact that there was nothing produced to 
indicate the history of the crime recorded at the time of admission 
to the hospital, which assumes relevance again for reason of the FIR 
having been registered on 18.05.2019, the next date of her 
admission. The explanation given by the brother is of tending to 
his sister admitted to the hospital, which cannot be accepted; 
especially since the hospital, on admission would have 
immediately intimated the police. 
12. Considering the above circumstances, we are unable to find 
the accused guilty of the offence alleged, especially noticing the 
discrepancies in the deposition of the victim, which does not align 
with that of the other witness, PW16 and the medical report. But for 
the deposition of the victim, there is nothing incriminating found 
against the accused. The vehicle is said to have been recovered by 

--- Page 60 ---
Page 8 of 8 
 
Ex. P7, seizure list as deposed by PW18 in whose name the same 
was registered. PW18 spoke of a sale having been carried out to 
the accused but the registration having not been changed. 
Pertinent is the fact that the IO did not speak of the seizure of the 
car nor was any examination carried out inside the car to find any 
telltale signs of assault complained of and the sexual intercourse 
carried out inside the car as alleged.  PW1’s testimony is not of the 
sterling character required for conviction on that sole basis.  
13. We are unable to sustain the conviction of the accused, who 
hence stands acquitted. He shall be released forthwith, if not 
required in any other case. If he is already on bail, then his bail 
bonds shall stand cancelled. 
14. The appeal is allowed. 
15. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand rejected.

193 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023

absolute.

--- Page 92 ---
unfortunately expired.
5. A claim petition was preferred by her parents
before the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal, which
awarded a compensation of Rs. 16,50,000/- along
with  interest  at  the  rate  of  9%  per  annum.
Aggrieved thereby, cross-appeals were preferred by
both the insurance company and the claimants before
the  High  Court.  The  High  Court  enhanced  the
compensation by Rs. 6,48,000/- in addition to the
amount awarded by the Tribunal, while reducing the
rate of interest from 9% to 6% per annum.
6. Learned counsel appearing for the appellants-
claimants has vehemently argued that the deceased
was a bright third-year B.E. (Computer Science)
student who had consistently secured first-division
marks in her semesters, and therefore, her notional
monthly income was erroneously assessed at a meager
sum of Rs. 15,000/- per month without properly
accounting for future prospects. It is further
submitted that the High Court erred in reducing the
rate of interest from 9% to 6% per annum without
assigning any reason whatsoever.
2

--- Page 93 ---
7. On the other hand, learned counsel appearing
for the respondent-Insurance Company has placed
reliance upon the judgment of this Court in "Smt.
Meena Pawaia & Ors. vs. Ashraf Ali & Ors." (Civil
Appeal No. 6724 of 2021, decided on 18.11.2021) to
contend that in comparable circumstances involving
a B.E. student, notional income was assessed at Rs.
10,000/- per month, and thus no further enhancement
is warranted.
8. This Court has carefully gone through the
aforesaid judgment and the record of the present
case. In "Smt. Meena Pawaia" (supra), the accident
had occurred in the year 2012, whereas in the
present case, the accident occurred on 18.08.2017.
Moreover, each case has to be adjudicated in its
own peculiar facts and circumstances.
9. Having heard learned counsel for the parties
and upon perusal of the record, this Court is of
the considered opinion that the courts below have
failed to properly assess the notional monthly
income and future prospects of a meritorious third-
year engineering student. In exercise of powers
3

--- Page 94 ---
conferred under Article 142 of the Constitution of
India, instead of undertaking separate calculations
under various heads, this Court is of the opinion
that the ends of justice would be subserved by
enhancing the total lump-sum compensation to Rs.
30,00,000/- (Rupees Thirty Lakhs only).
10. Further,  since  the  High  Court  has  not
assigned any cogent reason for reducing the rate of
interest from 9% to 6% per annum, the impugned
order to the extent it reduces the rate of interest
is also set aside, and the claimants are held
entitled  to  receive  the  entire  enhanced
compensation of Rs. 30,00,000/- along with interest
at the rate of 9% per annum from the date of filing
of the claim petition till realization.
11. The respondent-Insurance Company is directed
to deposit the entire amount as directed by this
Court, within a period of six weeks from today
before the MACT.
12. The  claimants  shall  furnish  their  bank
account details to the MACT so as to enable direct
electronic transfer of the compensation amount into
4

--- Page 95 ---
their bank account.
13. It is clarified that this order has been
passed in the peculiar facts and circumstances of
the present case.
14. With  the  aforesaid  observations  and
modification, the appeals stand allowed.
15. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand
disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO.5890 OF 2021
Sanjay Poddar & Ors.              ...Appellants
Versus
Niklesh Tirathdas Nihalani & Ors.                    ...Respondents
With
CIVIL APPEAL NO.5133 OF 2021
O R D E R
The 1st respondent in the above appeals who is the contesting
respondent  and  the  applicant  before  the  National  Company  Law
Tribunal  (NCLT)  had  challenged  the  transfer  and  transmission  of
shares  carried  out  by  the  Board  of  Directors  of  the  Company  in
violation of the Articles of Association.
2. The NCLT passed a common judgment in two applications filed
by  the  1st respondent,  against  which  the  appellants  herein
unsuccessfully  approached  the  National  Company  Law  Appellate
Tribunal (NCLAT). The matter was once reported as settled but again
the 1st respondent resiled from the settlement, which has resulted in
the matter being posted again before us. 
3. Dr.  A.M.  Singhvi,  learned  Senior  Counsel  appearing  for  the
appellants pointed out; from the additional documents filed to bring on

--- Page 113 ---
2
board the subsequent events, Annexure M, which is a declaration and
undertaking made by the 1st respondent on 27.06.2023. Therein, the
1st respondent had categorically stated that after due deliberations, an
undertaking is given that he does not wish to press the prayers before
the  NCLT  and  NCLAT  and  this  Court  may  pass  appropriate  orders
quashing order of the NCLAT. It was also undertaken that all claims
thereunder would be withdrawn, as a settlement has been reached in
all and every respect. 
4. From a bare reading of the declaration and undertaking, there
are no terms of settlement spoken of, but the general purport is that
the matter has been settled once and for all. It is fairly submitted by
the learned Senior Counsel for the appellants that only an amount of
Rs.2,11,34,000/- was paid as against the total share value of the 1st
respondent,  agreed  upon  at  Rs.3,76,60,000/-  in  instalments  up  to
05.04.2024.  The  1st respondent  refused  to  accept  the  balance
amounts, which has resulted in the stalemate. It is also pointed out
that the major portion of the settlement coming to Rs.1,43,34,000/-
was  paid  by  cheque  and  unfortunately  Rs.68,00,000/-  was  paid  in
cash. Fairly, it is submitted that the cash payment may be discounted
and  the  appellants,  to  bring  quietus  to  the  issue,  are  even  now
prepared to pay an amount of Rs.2,33,26,000/- within a period of one
week from today with interest as stipulated by this Court. 

--- Page 114 ---
3
5. Sri Anupam Lal Das, learned Senior Counsel appearing for the 1st
respondent, however, submits that the settlement was arrived at only
without reckoning the value of the immovable property, which was
sold for a song, which would, in fact, considerably increase the value
of the shareholdings. According to him, whatever money has been
received by him, would be deposited back with 9% p.a. interest and he
may be allowed to pursue the appeal, is the contention. 
6. We cannot but notice that as submitted by Dr. A.M. Singhvi, the
undertaking neither indicates the terms of the settlement nor puts
forth a further condition of satisfaction of the terms, in which event the
matter stands settled as on 13.05.2022. However, since it is submitted
by the appellants that the balance payment, though, they were ready
to pay, was not accepted by the 1st respondent, we are of the opinion
that  reasonable  interest  @  9%  p.a.  could  be  granted  to  the  1st
respondent.
7. In  the  above  circumstances,  we  direct  that  an  amount  of
Rs.2,33,26,000/- with 9% p.a. interest starting from 27.06.2023, the
date  of  declaration  and  undertaking,  shall  be  deposited  by  the
appellants before this Court, and on such deposit, the same shall be
disbursed to the 1st respondent forthwith after due verification. The 1st

--- Page 115 ---
4
respondent,  hence,  would  have  no  more  contentions  against  the
Company  or  the  appellants  and  his  claim  is  settled  and  satisfied
completely with respect to the family group he represents, as seen
from the order of the NCLAT.
8. The  6th respondent  represented  by  Sri  Navin  Pahwa,  learned
Senior Counsel, however, submits that there is a company petition
pending before the NCLT with respect to the sale of the immovable
property, which may be allowed to be pursued. We make it clear that
the settlement herein recorded applies to the 1st respondent and the
family group he represents and all other matters shall be agitated at
the appropriate forum, especially since the sale of the property was
not the subject matter of the instant proceedings before the NCLT or
NCLAT, which has resulted in the above appeals. 
9. On the settlement as above being recorded and set aside, the
orders of the NCLT and NCLAT challenged herein are set aside.
10. The appeals are disposed of.
11. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand rejected.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The present batch of cases raises concerns regarding the
selective use of video clips of court proceedings for commercial
gain, along with certain ancillary issues arising therefrom.
2. Vide an order dated 24.07.2026, this Court issued notice and
directed the Union of India to put up a proposal with respect to
the prayers made in the Writ Petition. Vide paragraphs 9 and 11 of
that order, the following interim directions were also issued:
“9. As an interim measure, it is directed that there
shall be no extraction, dissemination, monetisation,
posting,  re-posting,  uploading,  transmitting,
modification, storing, or hosting of the audio-video
recording(s) of the judicial proceedings on social media
5

--- Page 124 ---
or any other digital platforms without prior permission
of the Secretary General of the Supreme Court of India
or the Registrar Generals of the jurisdictional High
Courts.
xxx xxx xxx
11. However, it is clarified that this order shall have
no bearing on the reporting of Court proceedings by
recognized news outlets.”
3. These interim directions were reiterated on 09.10.2026 in the
following terms:
“5. Interim directions issued on 24.07.2026 prohibiting
extraction, dissemination, monetisation, posting, re-
posting, uploading, transmitting, modification, storing,
or  hosting  of  the  audio-video  recording(s)  of  the
judicial  proceedings  on  social  media  or  any  other
digital  platforms  without  prior  permission  of  the
Secretary General of the Supreme Court of India or the
Registrar Generals of the jurisdictional High Courts
shall  continue  to  operate  and  shall  be  faithfully
complied with by all social media channels.”
4. In deference to the previous orders, various High Courts have
filed their status reports. The learned Solicitor General of India
submits that the suggestions and recommendations made by the High
Courts, as well as the observations made by this Court in its
interim orders from time to time, are presently under consideration
of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY),
which is also examining the formulation of an appropriate policy in
this regard. While formulating the policy framework, MeitY shall
ensure strict compliance with the interim directions contained in
paragraph 9 of the order dated 24.07.2026, as clarified by the
subsequent order dated 09.10.2026. MeitY shall also put in place
6

--- Page 125 ---
appropriate measures to take action against those found to have
violated the said directions.
5. Post the matters on 25.11.2026.

                             O R D E R
Heard learned counsel for the parties.
2. The petitioners in all the cases are accused under
Sections 111, 314, 317(2), 317(4) of the Bharatiya Nyaya
Sanhita, 2023, under Section 7 of the Chhattisgarh Gambling
(Prohibition) Act, 2022 and under Sections 66(C) and 66(D) of
the Information Technology Act, 2000.
3. The allegation against the petitioners is that they
were part of a gang, which cheated people by luring them to
bet on games.
4. Learned counsel for the petitioners submits that the
petitioners were merely employed because of their skill in
software to facilitate the main perpetrators, who were the
master-minds and used to get some money out of it. It was
further submitted that the petitioners have no criminal
antecedents and the maximum sentence under Section 7 of the
Chhattisgarh Gambling (Prohibition) Act, 2022 is three years
and their case is also triable by the Magistrate and they
have been in custody for more than seven months.

--- Page 142 ---
5
5. Learned  counsel  for  the  respondent-State  of
Chhattisgarh submitted that the petitioners were part of the
gang and there has been recovery.
6. On  a  direct  query  to  learned  counsel  for  the
respondent-State of Chhattisgarh, it was not controverted
that the five so-called master-minds are still absconding and
that the petitioners are not master-minds in the present set
of transactions.
7. Having regard to the aforesaid factual aspect, we are
inclined to allow the prayer for grant of bail to the
petitioners. Accordingly, the petitioners be released on
bail, subject to such terms and conditions as may be imposed
by the Trial Court with a further condition that they shall
not commit any offence in future. Failure to comply with the
same may lead to cancellation of the present bail.
8. Accordingly, the Special Leave Petitions stand disposed
of.
9. Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall  also  stand
disposed of.

of the minor child being G.W.O.P. No.506 of 2020 before

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO. 9835/2017
THE STATE OF JHARKHAND & ORS.                Appellant(s)
                         VERSUS
   
UDAY NARAYAN MISHRA                    Respondent(s)
O R D E R
1. The present appeal, at the instance of the State
of Jharkhand, takes exception to the judgment dated 3rd
January, 2017, passed by the Division Bench of the
High Court of Jharkhand at Ranchi in L.P.A. NO.185 of
2016.
2. The Division Bench affirmed the order dated 11th
February, 2016, passed by the learned Single Judge in
W.P.(S) No. 4947 of 2015. The aforesaid writ petition
had been filed by the respondent who was serving as
the President of the District Consumer Forum, Palamu,
challenging  the  order  dated  21st September,  2015,
whereby he was removed from the post of President of
the District Forum.
3. We have heard and considered the submissions
advanced by learned counsel for the parties and have
gone through the material available on record.
1

--- Page 154 ---
4. The respondent was removed from the post for
purported misconduct defined in sub-rule (5)(e) of
Rule 3 of the Jharkhand Consumer Protection Rules,
2001, as adapted from the Bihar Consumer Protection
Rules, 1987. The relevant provision reads as follows:
“In addition to the provisions of Section 10(2),
State Government may remove from the office, the
President and member of a District Forum who-
(a) has been adjudged as insolvent, or
(b) has been convicted of an offence which in
the opinion of the State Government involves
moral turpitude, or
(c) has become physically or mentally incapable
of acting as such member, or
(d)  has  acquired  such  financial  or  other
interest as is likely to affect prejudicially
his functions as a member, or
(e) has so abused his position as to render his
continuance in office prejudicial to the public
interest:
      Provided that the President or member shall
not be removed from his office on the ground
specified in clauses (d) and (e) of the sub rule
(5) except on an enquiry held by the State
Government in accordance with such procedure as
it may specify in this behalf and finds the
member guilty of such ground.”
(Emphasis supplied)
5. Proviso  to  Rule  3  (5)  mandates  that  the
2

--- Page 155 ---
President or member shall not be removed from his
office on the grounds specified in clauses (d) and (e)
of the sub-rule (5) unless an enquiry is held by the
State Government in accordance with the procedure
specified by it and the State Government records a
finding that the member is guilty of the relevant
ground.
6. A  perusal  of  the  removal  order  dated  21st
September, 2015 (Annexure P-4) would make it clear
that not even a semblance of enquiry, what to talk of
an enquiry as contemplated under the proviso to Rule
3(5), was conducted before directing the removal of
the respondent from the post of President, District
Consumer Forum, Palamau. 
7. In  this  background,  we  find  no  reason  to
interfere  with  the  impugned  order  passed  by  the
Division Bench. There is yet another reason which
convinces us that the impugned order is not liable to
be interfered with. The rule contemplates that the
removal shall be exclusively within the domain of the
State  Government.  However,  the  order  of  removal
reflects that the decision to remove was taken by the
Chairman of the Selection Committee of the State
3

--- Page 156 ---
Consumer  Disputes  Redressal  Commission,  which  was
later  on,  approved  by  the  Departmental  Minister.
Hence, the decision for removal of the respondent
cannot  be  said  to  be  a  decision  of  the  State
Government.
8. The learned Single Judge, while allowing the
writ  petition  of  the  respondent,  permitted  the
appellants to initiate a fresh enquiry, if so desired.
However, as the respondent had already crossed the age
of 65 years in the year 2017, no useful purpose would
be served by permitting the appellants to initiate de
novo enquiry at this belated stage. Thus, the liberty
granted to the State to hold a de novo enquiry is set
aside.
9. In this view of the matter, we find no merit in
this appeal which is dismissed as such.
10. Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall  stand
disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO.12386/2024
JHARKHAND GRAMIN BANK   APPELLANT 
VERSUS
NARESH PRASAD & ORS.     RESPONDENTS
O R D E R
1. Naresh Prasad, the first respondent, was a cashier of the appellant-
Jharkhand  Gramin  Bank. He  was  proceeded  against  departmentally  on
allegations of financial irregularities committed by him in the discharge of
his duty as cashier. Charges were drawn up on 31st December, 2009. The
proceedings concluded with an order of penalty of removal from service
dated 18th July, 2012 being imposed on the first respondent. An appeal
carried from the order of penalty did not bear fruit. The order of removal
was affirmed by the appellate order dated 05th December, 2012.
2. Aggrieved thereby, the first respondent invoked the writ jurisdiction
of the High Court of Jharkhand at Ranchi1, albeit unsuccessfully. The writ
petition2 was dismissed by a Single Judge on 14th August, 2019. 
3.  However, the order of dismissal of the writ petition having been
1  High Court
2  W.P.(S) No. 6628 of 2013 
1

--- Page 159 ---
challenged  in  an  intra-court  appeal3,  the  first  respondent  emerged
successful. A Division Bench of the High Court by its judgment and order
dated 01st September,  2022  held the  disciplinary  proceedings  to have
been vitiated by reason of appointment of the same official as the Inquiry
Officer against whom the first respondent had earlier raised an objection
alleging bias and such objection had even been accepted by the Chairman
of  the  appellant-Bank. The  order  of  removal,  since  affirmed  by  the
appellate authority, was accordingly quashed.
4. The appellant-Bank has taken exception to the said judgment of the
Division Bench in this appeal by special leave, granted on 11th November,
2024.
5. During the pendency of the writ petition before the High Court, upon
attaining the age of superannuation, the first respondent retired on 10th
January,  2018.  However,  due  to  pendency  of  judicial  proceedings,  his
retiral dues have not been released.
6. Learned counsel appearing for the appellant-Bank, referring to the
decision  of  this  Court  in  Chairman,  Life  Insurance  Corporation  of
India and Ors. Vs. A. Masilamani4, is justified in his submission that the
High Court having quashed the order of removal due to a procedural flaw,
the  appellant-Bank  should  have  been  granted  liberty  to  resume  the
disciplinary proceedings from the stage the infirmity was identified.
7. Ordinarily, we would have followed the decision in  A. Masilamani
3  LPA No. 727 of 2019
4  (2013) 6 SCC 530
2

--- Page 160 ---
(supra)  and  directed  the  appellant-Bank  to  continue  the  disciplinary
proceedings against the first respondent from the stage of appointment of
an independent Inquiry Officer.
8. However, the facts of the case as presented before us now, do not
persuade us to follow the same course of action. The enormous lapse of
time  since the first respondent was charged with misconduct  and the
attending circumstances, mainly loss of evidence, fading memory and a
possible prejudice, cannot simply be brushed aside.
9. As noted, the charge-sheet is dated 31st December, 2009. Almost 17
years have elapsed since then. It would be difficult, both for the appellant-
Bank and the first respondent, to produce adequate and reliable evidence
in support of/to contest the charges. We are apprehensive, the inquiry
could be rendered an exercise in futility. A balance, therefore, has to be
struck. 
10. In our view, interest of justice would be sufficiently served if having
regard to the alleged amount of financial loss caused to the appellant-
bank by the first respondent, the same can be made good and the first
respondent receives his retiral dues. 
11. Thus, we proceed to direct as follows: -
(i) The appellant-bank is directed to release the retiral dues of the
first respondent, keeping apart a sum of Rs.33,000/- (being the
alleged financial loss suffered), within a period of two months from
date.
3

--- Page 161 ---
(ii) Since we have not examined the issues on merit, this order
shall not be read as an expression of opinion either upholding the
allegations  of  the  appellant-Bank  that  the  first  respondent  was
guilty  of  misconduct  and/or  that  the  first  respondent  had
committed no misconduct.
(iii) We  also  make  it  clear  that  since  the  first  respondent  was
proceeded against along with a Manager of the appellant-Bank, this
order shall not be cited as a precedent, if at all, the said Manager
has initiated proceedings against any final order of penalty and
such proceedings are pending before the competent court.
12. The appeal stands disposed of accordingly.
13. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand disposed of.
14. Parties shall, however, bear their own costs.
…….………………………….J.
(DIPANKAR DATTA)
……..………………………….J.
(SHEEL NAGU)
NEW DELHI; 
NOVEMBER 18, 2026.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA

  LOKESH KUMAR SINGHAL                               APPELLANT(S)

NAVEEN PORWAL & ORS.                               RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted. 
2. The present appeal is filed assailing the order of the High
Court dated 07.11.2025, in MCC Application No. 10511 of 2025
in Appeal from Order No. 208 of 2016, wherein, an application
was preferred by one Shri Rajesh Painuli, the present receiver
of the respondent No.6 – Trust, for filling up the coram by
appointing  two  persons  as  receivers  in  the  'panel  of
receivers'. The High Court, vide the impugned order dated
07.11.2025, instead of filling up the coram, appointed Shri
Badrinath and Shri Kedarnath Temple Committee (for short, the
'BKTC') as the receiver of the respondent No.6 – Trust.
Aggrieved by the same, the appellant is before this Court.
3. We have heard the learned Senior Counsel appearing for the
appellant  and  the  learned  counsel  appearing  for  the
respondents.

--- Page 164 ---
2
4. The short question for consideration is as to whether the High
Court can grant a relief which has not even been sought for by
the parties. In fact, in the application filed by the present
receiver, he sought for addition of two more receivers in the
panel for filling the coram. However, the High Court has
appointed BKTC as a receiver for respondent No.6 - Trust.
5. Though, the learned Senior counsel appearing for the appellant
raised an issue on the likelihood of bias, inasmuch as we are
remitting the matter to the High Court for fresh consideration
to decide by some other Bench, we are not inclined to go into
the said issue. Suffice it is to state, that the High Court
has exceeded its jurisdiction in passing the impugned order by
granting a relief which has not even been sought for by the
appellant. Besides this, no arguments in this regard have been
made by him.
6. In such view of the matter, the impugned order stands set
aside by making a request to the Hon’ble Chief Justice of the
High Court of Uttarakhand to assign this matter to any other
Hon’ble Judge to decide the MCC Application No.10511/2025 on
its merits, in accordance with the law, after affording an
opportunity of hearing to the parties concerned within a
period of three months from the date of receipt of a copy of
this order.  
7. We make it clear that BKTC is impleaded as party only for the
purpose of hearing them in the present appeal filed assailing

--- Page 165 ---
3
the impugned order. Thus, we make it clear that the BKTC shall
not be a party to the proceedings before the High Court.
However, all the issues which are to be raised are left open
for adjudication by the High Court. 
8. We also take note of the fact that respondent Nos.13 and 14
are no more, and there is no need to implead their legal
representatives, since this order is only limited to remitting
the matter to the High Court. In any case, they are the
trustees of the respondent No.6 - Trust. Thus, the fresh
trustee(s) can be impleaded. Therefore, it is open for the
High Court to take a call on the issue of new trustees
representing  legal  representatives  of  deceased  respondent
Nos.13 and 14.
9. The appeal stands disposed of, accordingly. 
10. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL No.        OF 2026
[arising out of SLP (Crl.) No. 17757 OF 2026]
SAYANTAN GUHA                                APPELLANT
                                VERSUS
THE STATE OF WEST BENGAL                     RESPONDENT
 
O R D E R 
1.   Leave granted.
2. By  the  impugned  judgment  and  order  dated  21st August,
2026, the High Court of Calcutta, Bench at Jalpaiguri has rejected
the appellant’s prayer for bail in anticipation of arrest.  
3. Appellant figures as an accused in FIR No. 0421 dated 12th
June,  2026  registered  with  Police  Station  Dinhata,  District-Cooch
Behar, West Bengal. It is alleged in the FIR1 that the appellant has
committed offences punishable under Sections 406, 420, 384 and
120-B of the Indian Penal Code, 1860.
4. We  have  heard  Mr.  Nagamuthu,  learned  senior  counsel
1 First Information Report

--- Page 186 ---
2
appearing for the appellant as well as Mr. Tushar Mehta, learned
Solicitor General of India appearing for the respondent-State of West
Bengal. We have also perused the documents on record including
the  statement  of  the  complainant  recorded  under  Section  183,
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023. 
5. The  allegation  against  the  appellant,  appearing  from  such
statement,  is  that  he  has  threatened  and  obstructed  the
complainant from approaching the police.  
6. It is not in dispute that the appellant is not named in the FIR.
His name surfaced in course of investigation. 
7. Taking an overall view of the matter in light of the allegations
against  the  appellant,  we  are  of  the  opinion  that  custodial
interrogation of the appellant is not necessary and that there is
sufficient ground for the appellant to be admitted to an order for
grant of bail in anticipation of arrest.
8. Accordingly,  the  impugned  judgment  and  order  stands  set
aside.
9. It is directed that in the event of the appellant being arrested
in connection with proceedings arising out of the aforesaid FIR, he
shall be released on bail by the arresting/investigating officer/trial
court on terms and conditions to be fixed by the trial court.
10. It is made clear that in the event the appellant breaches any
of the terms and conditions imposed by it, the trial court shall be at

--- Page 187 ---
3
liberty to cancel the bail of the appellant.
11. Needless  to  observe,  the  appellant  shall  not,  directly  or
indirectly, by making inducement, threat or promise, dissuade any
person acquainted with the facts of the case from disclosing such
facts to any police officer or to the court.
12. Also, since the investigation is yet to conclude, we direct that
if  the  investigating  officer  calls  upon  the  appellant  to  join  the
investigation, he shall do so by attending the police station.
13. We clarify that the observations made in this order and grant
of bail will not be treated as findings on the merits of the case.
14. The appeal is allowed on the above terms.
15.  Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

husband, Sagar Harendra Singh Kachhwah, was solemnized on 21st
April,  2014.  One  girl  child  was  born  to  the  petitioner  and  the

Pradesh. Records  of  Hindu  Marriage  Petition  No.94  of  2025  be
transferred to the transferee court immediately.

         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE VIJAY BISHNOI
For Petitioner(s) :Mr. Ankur Sood- 2083, AOR
                   Mr. Dhaman Trivedi, Adv.
                   Ms. Romila Mandal, Adv.
                   Mr. Prajwal Suman, Adv.
                                      
For Respondent(s) :Mr. Vikrant Rana, A.A.G.
                   Mr. Shaurya Sahay- 3311, AOR
                   Mr. Aman Jaiswal, Adv.
                   Ms. Sharvi Sharma, Adv.
                   Ms. Akanksha Pandey, Adv.
                   Mr. Manu, Adv.
                   Ms. Ayushi, Adv.
                   Ms. Bhawya Mishra, Adv.
                   
                   Mrs. Aishwarya Bhati, A.S.G.
                   Mr. Sudarshan Lamba- 3667, AOR
                   Ms. Shivika Mehra, Adv.
                   Ms. Chitrangda Rastravara, Adv.
                   Mr. Nasadiya Singh, Adv.
                   Mr. Rahul Bhaskar, Adv.
    Moulik Shrivastava, Adv.
    Ms. Khushbu Sinha, Adv.
                   
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The petitioner is facing prosecution and is on
bail. He held a passport which expired in the year
1

--- Page 194 ---
2022.
2. Having regard to the provisions of Section 6(2)
(f)  of  the  Passports  Act,  1967  read  with
Notification dated 25.08.1993, under Section 22 of
the  said  Act,  he  moved  an  application  seeking
permission to renew his passport and to travel
abroad.  The  specific  reason  disclosed  in  the
application was that petitioner’s wife is suffering
from  arthritis  and  requires  specialized  medical
treatment in the United States of America.
3. The Court of learned Magistrate rejected the
said application  vide order dated 15.07.2025 upon
finding that the application was not supported by
proper documents and the only medical document which
was submitted by the petitioner was in respect of
treatment of his wife in the year 2019. Further,
there was no medical certificate on record to show
that wife requires treatment in USA.
4. Aggrieved by the order passed by the High Court,
the petitioner filed an application under Section
482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 before
the High Court which came to be dismissed  vide
impugned order dated 27.10.2025.
5. The submission on behalf of the petitioner is
2

--- Page 195 ---
that unless the passport is renewed, concrete travel
plans cannot materialized; besides, he is not being
prosecuted for any serious offence that there is a
flight risk. He submits that the offences for which
the petitioner is being tried are punishable under
Sections 447, 323, 504 and 506 of the Indian Penal
Code,  1860  and  it  is  no  one’s  case  that  the
petitioner would be a flight risk. Besides, he has
placed reliance on a decision of this Court in
Mahesh Kumar Agarwal vs. Union of India and Anr.1
so as to contend that the petitioner has a right to
travel abroad and he could seek for renewal of his
travel documents.
6. We have gone through the materials available on
record and have considered the submissions made on
behalf of the petitioner.
7. What is important to note here is that the
petitioner has pressed the application specifically
on the ground that his wife requires treatment
abroad.  The  application  does  not  specifically
mention any other reason to travel abroad. In such
circumstances, when the trial court found that there
was no document to support such stand taken by the
petitioner,  the  application  was  not  found
1 2025 SCC OnLine SC 2887
3

--- Page 196 ---
acceptable.  Here  also,  the  petitioner  has  not
brought on record any medical documents or any other
need of the petitioner to travel abroad.
8. In such circumstances, we decline to interfere
with the impugned order.
9. However, we leave it open for the petitioner to
move a fresh application in case the petitioner has
any need for traveling abroad.
10. If  a  fresh  application  is  submitted  with
supporting documents, the same shall be accorded due
consideration without being prejudiced by rejection
of the earlier application.
11. With the aforesaid observations/direction, the
special leave petition is disposed of.
12. Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall  stand
disposed of. 
        
(CHETAN ARORA)                                  (MAYA KUMARI)

               S U P R E M E  C O U R T  O F  I N D I A
                       RECORD OF PROCEEDINGS
Writ Petition(s)(Civil) No(s).1493/2026
ALI MEHDI                                          Petitioner(s)
                                VERSUS
ELECTION COMMISSION OF INDIA & ORS.                Respondent(s)
Date : 19-11-2026 This petition was called on for hearing today.
CORAM :  HON'BLE THE CHIEF JUSTICE
         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE JOYMALYA BAGCHI
         HON'BLE MRS. JUSTICE V. MOHANA
For Petitioner(s) :Mr. Shariq Ahmed, Adv.
                   Mr. Muhammad Ali Khan, Adv.
                   Mr. Uday Bhatia, Adv.
                   Mr. Tariq Ahmed, Adv.
                   Mr. Tavleen Singh, Adv.
                   Mr. Adnan Yousuf, Adv.
                   M/s Ahmadi Law Offices- 3108, AOR
                                      
For Respondent(s) : 
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The petitioner, who claims to be an office bearer of a
political party, has invoked the writ jurisdiction under Article 32
of the Constitution of India, seeking directions for verification
of the allegedly false and fabricated Form-7 applications, stated
to have been filed during the Special Intensive Revision (SIR)
process in the Mustafabad Assembly Constituency of Delhi.
2. The petitioner primarily relies upon news reports published on
30.10.2026  and  05.11.2026,  wherein  it  was  reported  that  28
electors, against whom deletion applications had been filed, were
found to be physically residing at their given addresses.
3. The petitioner is said to have submitted a complaint to the
1

--- Page 206 ---
police authorities and forwarded representations to the Election
Commission of India (ECI) and the Chief Electoral Officer, Delhi,
highlighting the alleged fraudulent applications for deletion of
names from the electoral rolls and sought necessary action.
4. According to the petitioner, the District Election Officer,
North-East Delhi, subsequently conducted a verification exercise in
respect of 37 Form-7 applications attributed to one particular
Booth  Level  Agent  (BLA)/objector.  It  is  alleged  that,  upon
verification, 36 out of 37 applications were found to be false and
fabricated.
5. It is in these circumstances that the petitioner seeks the
following relief:
a) issue an appropriate writ, order or direction directing
the Election Commission of India, the Chief Electoral
Officer, Delhi and the concerned electoral authorities to
undertake and complete, through the competent statutory
machinery, a comprehensive verification and authentication
of  the  disputed  Form-7  applications  filed  in  AC-69
Mustafabad during the ongoing Special Intensive Revision,
including verification of the identity and authorship of
the persons shown as objectors and of the factual grounds
upon which deletion of electors has been sought;
b) direct that, pending completion of the aforesaid
exercise, no elector in AC-69 Mustafabad be deleted from
the electoral roll on the basis of any Form-7 application
whose authorship, authenticity or factual foundation is
disputed or has not been duly verified in accordance with
the  Representation  of  the  People  Act,  1950,  the
Registration  of  Electors  Rules,  1960  and  the  binding
instructions issued by the Election Commission of India.
c) direct the Respondents to forthwith preserve and secure
2

--- Page 207 ---
all  physical  and  electronic  records  relating  to  the
disputed  Form-7  applications,  including  the  original
applications,  mode  and  date  of  submission,
application/reference  numbers,  timestamps,  user/account
particulars, OTP or other authentication records wherever
applicable, and all other available audit trail capable of
establishing  the  provenance  and  authorship  of  such
applications;
d) direct the Respondents to ensure that no deletion
pursuant to a third-party Form-7 objection is effected
without proper verification of the grounds asserted therein
and strict compliance with the requirements of notice,
hearing  and  adjudication  prescribed  under  the
Representation of the People Act, 1950 and the Registration
of Electors Rules, 1960;
e) direct the Respondents to place before this Hon’ble
Court and make publicly available, in respect of AC-69
Mustafabad,  disaggregated  data  concerning  the  Form-7
applications received during the ongoing SIR, including the
total number received and disposed of; polling-part-wise,
objector-wise and ground-wise breakup; repeat objectors;
applications filed or facilitated through BLAs; cases where
the purported objector denied authorship or could not be
identified; applications found false or fabricated; notices
issued and served; action taken under Section 31 of the
Representation of the People Act, 1950; and the final
outcome of such-applications;
f) direct the Respondent Election Commission of India and
the Chief Electoral Officer, Delhi to examine the Form-7
applications received during the ongoing SIR across the NCT
of  Delhi  and  identify  instances  of  repeated  or  bulk
objections, concentration of applications in the names of
common objectors, or other comparable patterns warranting
scrutiny;
3

--- Page 208 ---
g) direct the Respondents to take appropriate action in
accordance with Section 31 of the Representation of the
People Act, 1950 and other applicable law;
h) Such other orders as may be necessary may also be
passed.
6. Since the petitioner has already submitted representations to
the Election Commission of India and the Chief Electoral Officer,
Delhi, we dispose of this petition, without expressing any opinion
on the merits of the allegations, with a direction to the aforesaid
authorities to examine and verify the grievances raised by the
petitioner  and  take  necessary  remedial  measures,  strictly  in
accordance with law.
7. Pending applications, if any, also stand disposed of.
(ARJUN BISHT)                              (PREETHI DILEEP KUMAR)

--- Page 233 ---

learned counsel appearing for the parties.

SUO MOTO CONTEMPT PETITION(CRIMINAL)  No(s).3/2026
[Arising out of impugned final judgment and order dated 27-01-2025
in RPFC No.16/2024 passed by the High Court of Kerala at Ernakulam]
IN RE: JAYAPRAKASH E.P.          Alleged Contemnor(s)/Petitioner(s)
                                VERSUS
                                                   Respondent(s)
[TO BE TAKEN UP AT THE TOP OF THE BOARD ALONG WITH THE RECORD OF
SLP(CRL.) NO. 1954/2026] 
 
Date : 23-11-2026 This petition was called for hearing today.
CORAM : 
         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE AHSANUDDIN AMANULLAH
         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE MANMOHAN 
       (By Courts Motion)
For Petitioner(s)   Mr. Jose Abraham- 2066, AoR  
                   
For Respondent(s)   Mr. Aljo K. Joseph, AoR                
          
                             O R D E R
Heard learned counsel for the parties.
2. In view of order dated 30.09.2026 passed by this Court in
SLP(Crl.) No.1954 of 2026, the Court had taken suo-motu notice and
issued contempt against the alleged contemnor/petitioner in the
main Special Leave Petition. The Court had also specifically
directed the alleged contemnor to be present in Court today.
3. Today, learned counsel for the alleged contemnor submitted
that the alleged contemnor has filed a motion, though the same is

--- Page 239 ---
2
not on record, that due to some medical issue, which we find to be
totally  frivolous,  the  exemption  from  personal  appearance  is
sought.
4. Be that as it may, the Court cannot allow such things to
happen, where a party/contemnor presumes an exemption on the basis
of letter circulated without even an interlocutory application
filed prior to the said date seeking exemption and getting a
specific order for exemption.
5. At this juncture, learned counsel for the alleged contemnor
submitted  that  the  alleged  contemnor  would  join  the  Court
proceedings through video conferencing. In view thereof, the matter
was taken up in the post-lunch session.
6. Having interacted with Mr. Jayaprakash E.P., who is the
alleged contemnor, we find that he has not understood the gravity
of his conduct and the Court does not appreciate the response from
him.
7. Even with regard to the next date of appearance, the grounds
on which the alleged contemnor tried to defer the same till the
next year, is nothing short of trying to take the Court for
granted.
8. In view thereof, we are constrained to issue non-bailable

ITEM NO.36               COURT NO.1               SECTION X
               S U P R E M E  C O U R T  O F  I N D I A
                       RECORD OF PROCEEDINGS
Writ Petition(s)(Civil) No(s).1446/2026
VIKAS SINGH BHADORIYA & ORS.                       Petitioner(s)
                                VERSUS
UNION OF INDIA & ORS.                              Respondent(s)
Date : 19-11-2026 This petition was called on for hearing today.
CORAM :  HON'BLE THE CHIEF JUSTICE
         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE JOYMALYA BAGCHI
         HON'BLE MRS. JUSTICE V. MOHANA
For Petitioner(s) :Mr. Sanjay M Nuli, Sr. Adv.
                   Mr. Govind Jee- 3275, AOR
                   Mr. Omanakuttan K K, Adv.
                   Mr. Gajjala Bhaskar, Adv.
                   Mr. Akhilesh Kumar Mishra, Adv.
                                      
For Respondent(s) : 
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The petitioners represent more than 4500 homebuyers in a
housing  project  known  as  ‘GM  Infinite  Global  Techies  Town’,
situated at village Thirupalya, Bengaluru, developed by respondent
nos. 4 - Gulam Mustafa Enterprises Private Limited, a private
builder-cum-developer. It is averred that the homebuyers have
already deposited 95% of the sale consideration/allotment price.
However, neither has the project been completed nor has possession
of the allotted apartments been handed over to them.
2. Meanwhile,  Corporate  Insolvency  Resolution  Process  (CIRP)
1

--- Page 248 ---
proceedings have been initiated against respondent no. 4 before the
Nation Company Law Tribunal (NCLT), Bengaluru. The petition was
admitted on 31.07.2026, resulting in the imposition of a moratorium
and appointment of an Interim Resolution Professional (IRP).
3. The petitioners apprehend that, on account of the pendency of
the CIRP proceedings, they are neither going to receive possession
nor a refund of the amount deposited by them. At the same time,
they apprehend that the banks with whom Tripartite Agreements were
executed may initiate coercive proceedings for recovery of the
outstanding amounts.
4. It  appears  to  us  that  if  the  petitioners  have  already
deposited a substantial portion of the allotment price, no coercive
action of any nature should be taken against them till the project
is  completed  and  the  possession  of  the  residential
unit(s)/apartment(s) is handed over of them.
5. Having regard to the fact that the project is situated in
Bengaluru, the CIRP proceedings are pending before NCLT, Bengaluru,
and the builder-cum-developer as well as the concerned financial
institutions are also stated to be located in Bengaluru, Karnataka,
we are of the view, that the appropriate and effective recourse for
the petitioners would be to approach the jurisdictional High Court
or NCLT, Bengaluru, as the case may be.
6. For abundant caution, we reiterate that no coercive action can
be  taken  against  the  petitioner-homebuyers  till  the  relevant
proceedings reach their logical conclusion. Ordered accordingly.
2

--- Page 249 ---
7. The Writ Petition is, accordingly, disposed of.
8. Pending applications, if any, also stand disposed of.
(ARJUN BISHT)                              (PREETHI DILEEP KUMAR)

material available on record.

was admittedly recovered from the possession of the
petitioner.  A  cash  amount  to  the  tune  of
Rs.8,70,000/- (Rupees Eight Lakh Seventy Thousand
only) was recovered from his possession, for which
the petitioner has tried to put up some explanation.
However,  validity  or  otherwise  of  the  said
explanation would have to be gone into at the trial.

contraband having been recovered from the possession
of the petitioner, we are inclined to extend the
indulgence of bail to him during the pendency of the
trial.

clarified  that  such  compliance,  to  be  effected  within  three  days,  would  be
without prejudice to the contentions of the parties. A subsequent order dated 8th
April, 2019 records that the interim order dated 7th September, 2018 is made
absolute in view of the appellant having joined the posting and that operation of
the charge memo dated 29th August, 2018 shall remain stayed.
4. Subsequent record of proceedings also reveal  that  a  contempt  petition
was moved by the appellant and that such petition was closed vide order dated
5th January, 2022 recording that the order of the Court had been finally complied
with.
5. Having  regard  to  the  facts  and  circumstances,  it  seems  that  nothing

--- Page 311 ---
2
would survive for decision upon the appellant demitting office on attaining the
age of superannuation, which usually is 60 years.
6. The civil appeals, accordingly, stand disposed of as infructuous, keeping
the question of law, if any, open.
7. Pending interlocutory application(s), if any, shall also stand disposed of.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The instant Writ Petition under Article 32 of the Constitution
of India has been filed purportedly in public interest seeking the
following reliefs:
“a) direction to the Election Commission of India to
verify the citizenship status of every applicant who
applies for inclusion in the electoral roll through Form 6
or Form 8 unless such verification has already taken place
in the SIR exercise.
b) set aside the ECI's decision dated 26.09.2026, and the
consequential directions dated 15.10.2026, insofar as they
dispense with or exclude the requirement of submission of
additional declaration prescribed under Annexure-IV to the
SIR Order dated 14.05.2026;
c)  direct  the  ECI  to  comply  with  its  Order  dated
14.05.2026 with Form-6 under the Registration of Electors
1

--- Page 317 ---
Rules, 1960, for inclusion in the electoral rolls and
revision exercises conducted after the SIR;
d) direct the ECI to obtain the declaration from all
applicants who have submitted their applications after the
SIR and permit them to submit their forms online as well
as through BLO;
e) alternatively, direct the Union of India to take apt
steps for purity of election rolls in order to ensure that
only citizens become electors;
f) pass such other order(s)/direction(s) as the Court
deems fit & proper.”
2. The petitioner’s main grievance is against the Press Note
dated 26.09.2026, in which the Election Commission of India has
clarified that during the non-Special Intensive Revision (SIR)
period,  only  the  forms  prescribed  under  the  Registration  of
Electors  Rules,  1960,  would  be  used  without  requiring  the
additional SIR declaration form.
3. The Election Commission of India subsequently issued an order
dated 15.10.2026 directing that in the Special Summary Revision of
electoral rolls, the applicants are permitted to seek inclusion
through the submission of statutory Form 6 without requiring the
additional declaration that is prescribed for SIR.
4. We have heard the petitioner-in-person.
5. Since,  the  issues  raised  by  the  petitioner-in-person
predominantly fall within the policy domain, for which an amendment
in the statute may be required, we dispose of this Writ Petition
without expressing any opinion on merits, with liberty to the
2

--- Page 318 ---
petitioner to forward a copy of this petition to the competent
authorities for their appropriate consideration and to enable them
to take necessary steps, in accordance with law.
6. The petitioner is directed to deposit the additional copies of
the paper book with the Registry and the Registry is directed to
forward the same to the respondents.
7. Pending applications, if any, also stand disposed of.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
